fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: in IPA transcriptions, the fieldworker uses [w] for [ɯ].]

item.description: [t̪u̟ɤɾəɣ] Quot.: “Chaneil tuaradh dha na bh’ann ann an diugh.” Note: quantity, number.
[ɡɑrɑṉ] Quot.: “Dean suidhe, a’ gharrain ghràinnde air do chasan!” Note: brat.
[nʹɛ̃vəɫ] Quot.: “’S e brod neamhall a bh’annsan.” Note: brat, rascal.
[ɑ:vəʴsɑð] Note: a person full of fun. [NOTES: the turned r used for the symbol which is unclear in the original.]
Quot.: “Tha e làn àbharsaireachd.” Note: He is full of fun.
[kɔ̃ṉəɫɔ:dʹ] Quot.: “Nach dean sibh air ar socair ’s sibh a deanamh [kɔ̃ṉəɫɔ:dʹ] dhan an tigh.” Note: putting the house into disarray.
[ˈdʹɛəd̪] Quot.: “Cha d’fhuair iad de dh’iasg na dheanadh [ˈdʹɛəd̪].” Note: the amount that would make one meal. (Different from “diathad” – accent on the [ɛ].)
[ʃĩṉ] Quot.: “ann a shineach” [hĩṉɑx]. Note: there.
[ʃid̪] Quot.: “ann a shiodach” [hid̪ɑx]. Note: there.
[ȷũ̜n̪ə] Quot.: “B’ionna dha fuireach na dhachaidh fhéin.” Note: He would be better to stay in his own home.
[pe:tʹɑṉɑx] Note: the fibres which can be pulled from dry spongy peat, sometimes smoked by boys. Known in Barvas as “calcas”.
Quot.: “Rinn mi tòrr cuartlanaich.” Note: moving about.
[spɛ:c] Quot.: “Tha spèic mhath eadar so ’s an eaglais.” “Tha e spèic mhath as.” Note: a good distance.
[nʹũ̜:ʴsṯɑṉ] Note: Mrs. MacA’s pronunciation of the word for the celebration drink given on the birth of a child. [NOTES: the turned r used for the symbol which is unclear in the original.]
Note: tall grass growing in lochs.
Quot.: “Mhì-chòrd Nis rithe.” Note: She didn’t like Ness.
[ɫɑ̃:vəɡɑṉiç] Quot.: “Cha bhiodh e a’ deanamh obair throm ach bhiodh e a’ làmhaganaich timchioll.” Note: doing little jobs.
Quot.: “Bhiodh e a’ gearraghobaich rium.” Note: sharp-witted banter.
Note: forked strips of land.
[sɑ̃vəɫ] Quot.: “Chan fhaca mi air a shamhal e bho’n uairsin.”
[ı:k] Note: a triangular piece of cloth inserted, e.g. into the sides of a skirt to make it wider.
Quot.: brogan Sàboint. Note: best shoes for Church wear.
Quot.: léine-caitheamh. Note: working shirt.
Quot.: léine-chriomaidhean [lʹe:ṉəˈxɾw̃miɑn]. Note: old-fashioned collarless striped men’s shirt.
Quot.: Tha an tigh aige ann an clais a’ rathaid. Note: His house is just beside the road.
Quot.: “’S e obair gun bhiadh gun thuarasdal a th’agad.” Note: useless, pointless work.
[st̪ɑ:ðɑxk] Quot.: “a’ stàireachd air a’ rathad”. Note: walking with no apparent aim in view.
Quot.: “Nam biodh mo dhà chrann na mo làmh…” Note: If I had the choice…
[sɡu̟dʹəlɑðɑxk] Note: messing about with water.
[spɑd̪əðɑxk] Quot.: “Tha e làn dhan a’ spadaireachd.” Note: vanity, usually as regards one’s appearance.
Quot.: “Bha suathalas aice rithe.” Note: She resembled her somewhat.
[d̪ɾɑvɑlʹtʹ] Note: wooden canopy put over a fire against the wall before chimneys were built.
Quot.: lobhta poc. Note: ceiling of sacking in black houses.
Note: grate put on top of the hearthstone when the fire was in the middle of the floor. Considered at the time to be a big advance.
Quot.: “Tha do bhiadh air a dhol na ruadhan air an teine.” Note: food spoiling on the fire.
Quot.: an teasach dhearg. Note: scarlet fever.
Quot.: Bithidh e a’ cur conas orm. Note: It/He annoys me.
Quot.: “Is maith a’ sgàthan suil caraid.”
[ku̟ɤɾəɣ] Quot.: “Cuaradh ormsa! Carson a rinn mi siod?”
Quot.: “’S e duine rathail aig nach bi sin ri phàigheadh.” Note: in the sense of fortunate.
[t̪ɑɾɑɡʹəd̪əðɑk] Note: passing remarks designed to incite the person at whom they are aimed.
[kɑɫə] Quot.: Có am ministear dhan tug sibh calla? Note: a “call” to a congregation.
Quot.: cluasan na prais. Note: the loops on either side of the pot to which the “bùlais” is attached.
Note: sleet.
[bɑɫɑʃtʹ] Note: ballast.
Quot.: duine ballaisteach. Note: a solid, sensible person. (Also: “Chaneil móran ballaist anns an duine ud.”)
[fɔitʹɑɡ] Quot.: “Foiteag, foiteag, ’s e a tha fuar.” or “Foiteag, tha e teth.” Note: “foiteag” used in connection with heat usually when touching a hot object. Not used as regards hot weather.
[ˈtʹıtʹɑɡ] Note: exclamation used by a person who is wetted, e.g. by a splash.
[fɤʴṉḏɑð] Note: Mrs MacA’s pronunciation of “furniture” in Gaelic. [NOTES: the turned r used for the symbol which is unclear in the original.]
Quot.: “Nach àluinn na copanan sìna a tha sin.” Note: china.
[pðıʃtʹɑɫ] Quot.: a’ chlann a’ cluich le pristealan. Note: bits of broken cups, plates, saucers, etc.
Quot.: ’S iad a fhuair a’ rotach. Note: in the sense of a good following wind when sailing.
Quot.: seacanaich na Samhna. Note: a calm spell of weather in November. Houses were thatched at this time. (Put also under Samhainn.)
Quot.: garraiseach na Bealltainn. Note: an annual spell of bad weather.
[mɑ̃ʴsṯɑṉiç] Quot.: na màrtanaich. Note: hacks on the feet caused by going barefoot early in the year. [NOTES: the turned r used for the symbol which is unclear in the original.]
[d̪ɾu̟:kɑṉ] [d̪ɾu̟kɑṉ] Note: hacks under the joints of the toes caused by going barefoot.
[rwfɑṉiç] Note: skin breaking behind the nails.
Note: the root or core of a boil.
[d̪ɑɾəs] Quot.: “Bha mu dhusan dorus air a’ niosgaid.” Note: break in a boil where the pus comes out.
Note: a spot, usually boggy, where animals are lost.
Note: a line of stepping-stones across a stream.
Quot.: “Rinn na caoraich stàdhar uamhasach dheth.” Note: ground churned into mud by the trampling of sheep.
Quot.: “Thainig fàireag an ceann a shliasaid.” Note: applied to a swollen gland.
[sɑ:ləɡɑṉ] Note: water-brash.
[ru̜:rɑ:] Quot.: “Tha sibh air rùdh-ràdh a dheanamh dhan an tigh.” Note: everything upside down.
[kõərɑ:] Quot.: “am beul a’ chomha-thràth”. Note: at nightfall.
[d̪u̜ru̜ɣ] Quot.: “’S ann durgh a tha cridhe fear dha m’ fheadhainn / mo leannan.” Note: dour. This was usually said by a girl or woman when the fire wasn’t taking properly.
Quot.: “O, well, tha thu aig saorsainn do thoil a réisd!” Note: “O, well, please yourself then!”
[st̪ɤɾɤliç] Note: noisy commotion.
[sw:vəɫ] Quot.: “Chan fhaca tu càil air an t-saoghal [t̪w:vəɫ] collach ris.” Note: “saoghal” often pronounced this way here.
Quot.: “Chuir e neònachas orm.” Note: It puzzled me.
Quot.: “’S ann air cùl a’ ghàraidh a tha sinne.” Note: We are outside the township boundary. (Put also under gàradh.)
Quot.: “Chan urrainn dha e fhéin ullanachadh.” Note: said of a person in bed who cannot make himself more comfortable in bed.
[eðɑpiʃ] Quot.: “Tha e làn eireapais.” Note: full of quirks, fads.
[fɑɾɑɾɑm] Note: nickname. (Pronunciation.)
Quot.: “Tha sin a’ toirt innseadh dhuit man a bha.” Note: That lets you know how things were.
Note: lair in a cemetery.
Quot.: “Ròineagan a’ tuiteam fon an t-snàth.” Note: short wool fibres falling from yarn.
Quot.: “Ach ’s e is [d̪ɔrə] dhomh nach leur dhomh rud sam bith.” Note: “But what is hardest on me is that I cannot see anything.”
Quot.: “Fortan an cois an dòrtadh, pòsadh an cois a’ losgadh.”
Quot.: “Cha toir duine a mhóintich e.” Note: No-one will get the better of him, fool him.
[kɔ̃ṉəd̪əlɑx] Note: a sheep strayed from another pasture on to one’s own.
Quot.: “Theab i mo liathadh.” Note: She nearly gave me grey hairs (metaphorically speaking).
Quot.: “Chuir i mo shùil a mach.” Note: said by a girl when a rival had taken over her boyfriend.
Note: pronounced [ʃu̟:ʃə].
